analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare drug plans to cover cheaper generics and biosimilars at lower cost than the brand-name originals.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to make Medicare drug plans preferentially cover cheaper generics and biosimilars — introduced with two cosponsors — has sat in two House committees with no action since March 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require stand-alone Medicare Part D drug plans that use formularies to place any cheaper generic version of a drug, and at least two cheaper biosimilar copies of a biologic, on a better coverage tier with lower out-of-pocket costs than the brand-name original. It would also ban plans from using hurdles like prior authorization or step therapy against those cheaper copies if the hurdles don't apply to the brand drug. The rules would take effect for plan years starting January 1, 2027.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors and people with disabilities enrolled in stand-alone Medicare Part D plans, who would get guaranteed access to cheaper generic drugs and biosimilars on better formulary tiers and lower out-of-pocket costs than the brand-name versions, without extra hurdles like prior authorization or step therapy that plans sometimes apply to the cheaper product but not the brand. Generic and biosimilar drug makers would also gain guaranteed preferred placement for their products.

how_it_helps.text: Requires Part D prescription drug plans that use formularies to include, in a preferred position — a more favorable tier with lower patient out-of-pocket costs — every covered generic drug whose wholesale acquisition cost is below that of its brand-name reference drug.
Requires those plans to include at least two biosimilar biological products in a preferred position whenever their wholesale acquisition cost is below the cost of the reference biologic.

Bars plans from imposing access limits on the required generics and biosimilars — including prior authorization or step therapy — that are more restrictive than what applies to the brand-name reference drug, or that otherwise reduce enrollees' access to the cheaper product relative to the brand.
Applies to plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2027, so the protections would start quickly if enacted.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers would bear the main cost, losing sales when plans must give preferred placement to cheaper generic and biosimilar versions. Part D plan sponsors and the pharmacy benefit managers that run their formularies would lose the utilization-management tools and brand-favoring formulary placements they currently use, which are tied to the rebate system built around high-list-price brands. A share of any lost rebate revenue could be reflected in plan premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers, PBMs, Part D plans

drawbacks.text: The bill compares list prices (wholesale acquisition cost) rather than the net prices plans actually pay after rebates, and it constrains the utilization-management tools plans use; plans and PBMs could respond by shifting some lost rebate revenue into premiums or reduced benefits for Part D enrollees.

The requirement applies only to stand-alone Part D prescription drug plans (PDP sponsors) and not to the drug coverage inside Medicare Advantage plans, leaving most Medicare beneficiaries without the same protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors who take drugs with cheaper generic or biosimilar versions available, the bill is a clear win: guaranteed lower-cost coverage without extra red tape, at a cost borne mainly by brand-name drug makers and the rebate system around them. Its main honest weakness is scope — it covers only stand-alone Part D plans, not Medicare Advantage drug coverage, and it could modestly nudge premiums if plans lose rebate revenue they currently capture by steering patients toward expensive brands.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to two House committees, where it has sat with no hearings, no markup, and no vote so far this Congress.

narrative.text: Representative Doris Matsui introduced the bill on March 27, 2026, joined by Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks, a Republican, and Representative Jake Auchincloss, a Democrat, as original cosponsors.
The same day, the House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and also to the Ways and Means Committee, the standard step that lets committees review a bill before any floor vote.
No further action is recorded — no committee consideration, no vote, and no movement in either chamber since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one's situation has changed: the bill is stalled early. If it stays parked, brand-name drug makers and pharmacy benefit managers are better off because the current formulary and rebate system — which favors high-priced brand drugs — stays in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and PBMs, so far

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is bipartisan — one Democrat, one Republican, and one more Democrat — but no committee or floor votes have occurred, so the partisan shape of actual support is unknown.

industries.note: The bill forces Part D plans to give preferred, lower-cost placement to cheaper generics and biosimilars instead of their brand products, cutting sales of the expensive originals. Their interest runs against the enrollees who would pay less at the pharmacy.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and Part D plan sponsors
industries.note: The bill strips plans of formulary steering and utilization-management tools used to favor high-list-price brands, which sit at the center of the rebate system PBMs and plans profit from. Some lost rebate revenue could flow into premiums, but the direct effect on them is a loss of control.

Their products get a guaranteed preferred formulary position and protection from extra access hurdles whenever they cost less than the brand, expanding their market. Their gain comes directly from patients paying less.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has two cosponsors and two committee referrals with no recorded activity since March 2026, and the Congress runs through January 3, 2027. The most likely path is that it dies in committee, as most bills do; its realistic chance is being folded into a larger Medicare or drug-pricing package rather than getting its own vote.
